records.title: Buy your Mining Machinery from Whitmore & Sons
content: Welcome to the Whitmore & Sons Mining Machinery information page!  Brian Whitmore, your head of company wishes to give you a warm salute and welcome to our space on the world wide web.  Every generation of Whitmore right back to the company's founding in 1798 has contributed to the company you see today, and the quality of our products are thanks in great part to these tireless efforts from our family, and the best products of all are in our mining range.  Try our Mine Carts, the best materials are used, right from today, as far back as 1840 to the Black Pine Silver Mine, its all thanks to us and our superior machinery!

The only family members who can not claim this accolade are Grandpa Arthur and Uncle Harry!  The irony is though, one did do some work in a mine that used our machinery, but after it had closed, as a Police Sergeant, leading a search party investigation, and the other wrote a book about wacky things found in dark unexpected places like abandoned mines!  Still, they are one of us and they excelled at what they did!

records.title: An Important and Historic Club
content: The Honey Dew Caving Club was a small Saskatchewan-based caving society founded in 1902 by Thomas O'Rourke, bringing together a group of enthusiastic amateur explorers interested in the province's underground landscapes. Though modest in size, the club undertook numerous expeditions during its ten years of activity, documenting cave entrances, passages and underground formations that had received little formal attention. Among its most notable achievements was an unofficial survey and hand-drawn mapping of a substantial portion of the Black Pine Cave System, work that later proved useful to subsequent explorers.

The club's activities came to an abrupt end following the death of O'Rourke in 1911, when he was killed in an abseiling accident while travelling in France. Without its founder and principal organiser, the Honey Dew Caving Club gradually ceased operations and was formally considered defunct by 1912. Despite its short existence, the club left behind a reputation for enthusiastic exploration and careful observation, with surviving notebooks and sketches providing a curious glimpse into Saskatchewan's early amateur caving community.

They were most famous for the 1912 release of the Black Pine Cave System Collective Map, created through the life of the club by its main members, not least Thomas who had a fixation on the System, largely due to his police work searching for the missing Askew Spencer.
